01.r: Draws the conclusion from what Paul has just said.
01.n: Abbott-Smith calls it a consecutive particle: it states a result.

02.r: What the reader once was, he is not now.
02.n: The negative οὐ joined to ἔτι, 'still': 'no longer'. The DRC's 'now ... not' most likely follows its Latin source.

03.r: Singular: Paul speaks to each reader in turn.
03.n: Second person singular, though the letter is to many. The DRC alone reads 'he is'.

04.r: One owned by another, with no claim on the household's goods.
04.n: This study renders δοῦλος 'slave'. The KJV, Geneva, DRC and YLT say 'servant' and the ASV 'bondservant'. That a slave cannot inherit is the contrast the verse draws, not a point a lexicon states.

05.r: Sets the new standing against the old.
05.n: A strong 'but': not this, but that.

06.r: A son of the household, with a son's rights.

07.r: Takes the condition as true: you are a son.
07.n: A condition assumed to be fact, which is why the BSB says 'since'.

08.r: Carries the argument one step further.

09.r: Repeats the word to build on it.
09.n: The Greek has no verb in this clause: 'and if a son'.

11.r: One who will receive what belongs to the father.
11.n: Abbott-Smith builds the word from κλῆρος, a lot, and νέμομαι, to possess. He gives first 'an heir', and then a sense used of those who as sons of God inherit the privileges of the Messianic Kingdom.

12.r: God is the one through whom the heirship comes.
12.n: See the note on the text: the KJV's Greek reads 'through Christ'.

tr_note: The Textus Receptus adds Χριστοῦ, 'Christ', and has διά, 'through', in another position, giving 'an heir of God through Christ'. That is the KJV's reading, followed by the Geneva and YLT; the DRC, ASV and BSB, like our text, read 'an heir through God'.
